Tough
TUF
adjective (Boomer slang)
From Old English tóh, firm, tenacious. The ordinary senses — strong, hard to break or chew, difficult, rough — are old (Webster 1828). As teen slang of the 1950s and early 1960s, tough also meant excellent, sharp, impressive ("a tough car," "tough threads"), especially in the greaser and hot-rod culture; alongside it ran tough as an insult for a hoodlum ("a bunch of toughs") and the dismissive tough luck / tough!

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In 1950s and 60s teen slang, tough meant sharp, cool, impressive: a tough car, a tough jacket. It also named a kind of young man — the greaser in the leather jacket, the tough guy who did not cry. The Christian observation: Scripture wants men to be tough, but in a different way and for a different reason. Paul writes, "Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ" (2Ti 2:3), and "Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong" (1Co 16:13). God told Joshua, "Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest" (Jos 1:9). That is real toughness: endurance, courage, standing fast. But the world’s tough guy is often brittle — hard on the outside to protect what is fragile inside, unable to weep, to confess, or to be gentle. Scripture’s strong man is also tender: "be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you" (Eph 4:32). And his toughness does not come from himself: "when I am weak, then am I strong" (2Co 12:10). The toughest Man who ever lived set His face toward Jerusalem knowing what waited, and also took children in His arms. A father who wants a tough son should show him both.

Webster 1828 Definition

1950s–60s teen slang for sharp, impressive, cool — on the 1828 root "firm, tenacious" — a toughness Scripture commands (2Ti 2:3; 1Co 16:13) but joins to tenderness (Eph 4:32) and to strength made perfect in weakness (2Co 12:10).

TOUGH, adj. (Boomer teen slang, 1950s–60s) Excellent, sharp, impressive. "That’s a tough car." n. A rough, aggressive young man; a hoodlum. Tough luck! / Tough! — too bad.

Webster (1828) — TOUGH, adjective tuf. 1. Having the quality of flexibility without brittleness; yielding to force without breaking. The ligaments of animals and of India rubber are remarkably tough tough timber, like young ash, is the most proper for the shafts and springs of a carriage. 2. Firm; strong; not easily broken; able to endure hardship; as an animal of a tough frame. 3. Not easily separated; viscous; clammy; tenacious; ropy; as tough phlegm. 4. Stiff; not flexible.

Decode for families: the greaser’s "tough" is the ancestor of every later word that praises hardness — badass, savage, alpha.

Key Scripture

2Ti 2:3 — "Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ."

1Co 16:13 — "Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong."

Jos 1:9 — "Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest."

2Co 12:10 — "Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong."

Eph 4:32 — "And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you."

Modern Corruption

The tough-guy ideal prizes hardness and hides weakness; Scripture commands endurance and courage but roots them in God’s strength and joins them to a tender heart.

expand to see more

The 1950s tough — James Dean, Marlon Brando, the leather-jacketed greaser — was a rebel against suburban softness, and there was something right in the protest. A culture that produces men who cannot endure hardness is in trouble. But the tough-guy image confused toughness with coldness. It taught boys that strength means never needing anyone, never admitting fault, never showing grief. That is not strength; it is armor over a wound, and it breaks marriages.

The biblical man is tougher than the greaser and softer than the suburbanite. He endures hardness as a soldier (2Ti 2:3) and weeps at a friend’s grave. He stands fast in the faith (1Co 16:13) and forgives as he has been forgiven (Eph 4:32). And he knows his strength is borrowed: "when I am weak, then am I strong" (2Co 12:10). That is the only toughness that lasts past forty.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English tóh (tenacious, firm) → English tough (strong, hard, difficult) → 1950s–60s teen slang tough (excellent, sharp); a tough (a hoodlum).

Old English tóh — tenacious, sticky, firm

English tough — strong, not easily broken; hard to chew; difficult

19th c.: a tough — a rough, a ruffian

1950s–60s greaser and hot-rod slang: tough — excellent, sharp

Greek krataioō — to be strong (1Co 16:13); kakopatheō — to endure hardship (2Ti 2:3)
